verdict: Complementary. CSF 2.0 states outcomes anyone may use; ISO/IEC 27001 is a management system standard that an accredited body certifies.

rows.label: Purpose
rows.a: One shared language for cybersecurity outcomes, from the board to the operations floor.
rows.b: The international standard for running information security as a managed system, and one you can be certified against.

rows.label: Who Must Follow It
rows.a: Voluntary by design. Executive Order 13800 directs every federal agency head to use it.
rows.b: Voluntary. It binds where a contract, a customer or a regulator asks for conformity or certification.

rows.label: How It Is Assessed
rows.a: No certification and no assessor. An organization describes itself with Profiles and Tiers.
rows.b: An accredited certification body audits in two stages, then returns for surveillance and recertifies on a three-year cycle.

rows.label: Its Text
rows.a: Free from NIST, and shown here in full.
rows.b: Sold by ISO and national standards bodies. Lensatic shows its shape and none of its text.

connect: NIST’s CSF 2.0 Reference Tool prints, beside each Subcategory, the ISO/IEC 27001:2022 clauses and Annex A controls that relate to it. They are NIST’s pointers, not an equivalence, and a certificate does not prove the outcomes.
noScore: Lensatic gives no strictness score here. One describes outcomes and the other is certified, so neither is stricter than the other. Many organizations use both.
overlapLine: Counted from NIST’s own references. Open a Function, then a Category and a Subcategory, to see the identifiers NIST names. Lensatic shows none of ISO’s text.
